In the agricultural college near Hisar, Lalit's group had a field report due on Monday: soil moisture from ten plots. On Saturday, Lalit was supposed to take the readings from plot seven. He went to a cousin's engagement instead.
On Sunday night, the group sheet had a blank for plot seven. Sarika messaged, "Lalit? We need your number."
Lalit looked at plots six and eight. He typed a number in between. It looked right. He told himself, "Everyone fudges one reading. It won't change anything."
It did. Plot seven turned out to be the one plot where a new irrigation method had been tried. The group's conclusion, that the method made no difference, rested partly on his invented number.
Their teacher praised the report. Lalit felt the praise land like a stone in his stomach.
That evening, he went to Sarika's room. "I need to tell you something about plot seven," he said.

qa.q: Which plot's reading did Lalit invent?
qa.a: Plot seven.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel when the teacher praised the report?
qa.a: Lalit felt guilty, the praise landing like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: What is the right next step for Lalit, and why?
qa.a: Telling Sarika and the teacher, then taking the real reading, because the invented number changed the group's conclusion about the new method.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel when Lalit tells her?
qa.a: Sarika would likely feel shocked and let down, since the whole group's report depended on the data being real.

grounding: Illustrates a student who fabricates a data point to meet a group deadline, telling himself everyone does it, while the harm is real.

subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
passage:
In Copenhagen, Hana's group presented their urban design project to the professor on Friday. Anders had made the key slides: the traffic flow maps, three late nights of work. But Anders had a fever and couldn't come.
Hana presented them. When the professor said, "These maps are excellent. Who made them?", Hana hesitated. The group had agreed to present as a team. She said, "We worked on them together."
It wasn't quite a lie. Everyone did it. Groups share credit. She told herself this on the bike home.
On Monday the professor emailed Hana, not Anders, to invite her to a summer research project on traffic design. Hana read it three times. Her stomach tightened.
When Anders came back, he saw the email on the group chat. He didn't say much. "Congratulations," he wrote, and then went silent for two days.
Hana sat with her laptop open, a reply to the professor half typed: "I should tell you who really made those maps."

qa.q: What slides had Anders made?
qa.a: The traffic flow maps.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when the professor's email arrived?
qa.a: Hana felt guilty and uneasy, her stomach tightening because the credit belonged to Anders.

qa.q: What should Hana do now, and why?
qa.a: Tell the professor that Anders made the maps, because staying silent keeps taking an opportunity that is his.

qa.q: How might Anders feel seeing the email?
qa.a: Anders likely feels hurt and passed over, which is why he writes a flat "Congratulations" and goes silent.

grounding: Shows a student who lets a teammate's uncredited work pass as shared or her own, rationalising it while the harm to him is real.

subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
passage:
In the biology lab, Yamini's group had to submit their enzyme experiment by five. At 3:30, one of the six readings was clearly wrong: it made the graph jump.
There was no time to repeat it. Saurabh, her lab partner, was already typing the conclusion. "Just smooth it," he said. "Put something that fits."
Yamini hesitated, then typed a number that made the curve neat. Everyone did small things like this, she told herself. It was one reading out of six.
The report got an A.
In April, the lab instructor asked their group to repeat the experiment as a demo for the juniors. Yamini's hands were cold as they set it up. The real readings came out, and the curve jumped again, just where it had before. The instructor frowned. "Your report shows a smooth curve. What happened?"
Saurabh looked at the floor. Yamini felt her face burn. "I changed one reading," she said quietly. "I'm sorry."

qa.q: How many readings did the experiment have?
qa.a: One reading out of six.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel as they set up the demo in April?
qa.a: Yamini felt anxious and guilty, her hands cold because she knew the real reading might expose the change.

qa.q: What could Yamini and Saurabh have done at 3:30 instead?
qa.a: Reported the odd reading honestly and noted there was no time to repeat it, rather than inventing a number.

qa.q: How might the instructor feel after Yamini's admission?
qa.a: The instructor would likely be disappointed but may respect that Yamini finally told the truth.

grounding: Illustrates a student who fabricates a data point to meet a deadline, softening the guilt with 'everyone does it', until the real data exposes it.

subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
Something has been sitting on my chest since Thursday, and you're the only one far enough away to tell.
Our group presented the water survey project. Ravi did the whole analysis, the charts, the regression, everything, but he was down with fever and missed the presentation. I presented his section. When Dr Menon asked who built the model, I said, "We worked on it together," and she looked straight at me and said, "Excellent work, Sangeeta." I just said thank you.
Everyone does this, right? Group marks are group marks. Ravi won't even know. That's what I keep telling myself at night, and it works for about ten minutes.
Except the individual marks count towards the grade. And Ravi is applying for the research assistant post, and Dr Menon is the one choosing.
I think I have to write to her. I've opened the email four times.
Love,
Sangeeta

qa.q: Who did the analysis for the project?
qa.a: Ravi did the whole analysis, the charts, the regression, everything.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel, despite the "everyone does this" excuse?
qa.a: Only briefly: Sangeeta still feels guilty, with something sitting on the chest, and the excuse works for about ten minutes.

qa.q: What should Sangeeta write to Dr Menon?
qa.a: A short, honest email saying Ravi built the model and did the analysis, so the individual marks and the research post credit the right person.

qa.q: How might Ravi be affected if Sangeeta says nothing?
qa.a: Ravi could lose individual marks and a fair chance at the research assistant post, since Dr Menon believes Sangeeta did the work.

grounding: Shows a student letting a teammate's uncredited work pass as their own and using everyone-does-it to soften the guilt.
